ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Autoinduction

A 34-year-old man starts carbamazepine at a stable daily dose. Over the next several weeks, its elimination half-life becomes shorter despite adherence and unchanged kidney function. Which pharmacokinetic property best explains this change during continued therapy?

  1. Inhibition of its own metabolic enzymes
  2. Induction of its own hepatic metabolism
  3. Progressive saturation of all renal filtration
  4. Irreversible accumulation in bone
  5. Loss of all oral absorption after the first dose
Answer and explanation

Induction of its own hepatic metabolism

Carbamazepine autoinduces metabolizing enzymes, increasing clearance over the initial weeks.

Option explanations

Induction of its own hepatic metabolism: Carbamazepine autoinduces metabolizing enzymes, increasing clearance over the initial weeks.

Progressive saturation of all renal filtration: Carbamazepine autoinduction is hepatic, not saturation of filtration.

Irreversible accumulation in bone: This would not explain a shorter elimination half-life.

Loss of all oral absorption after the first dose: Oral absorption does not normally cease.

Inhibition of its own metabolic enzymes: Inhibition would tend to reduce clearance.
